what_its_for: Insulin glulisine is a fast-acting insulin used to control blood sugar levels in adults and children (4 years and older) with type 1 or type 2 diabetes. It works right around mealtime to prevent your blood sugar from rising too high after you eat.
how_to_take: Inject insulin glulisine under the skin (subcutaneously) in your stomach area, upper arm, or thigh. You can also use it through an insulin pump. Rotate your injection sites each time to avoid skin problems like lumps or thickening. Do NOT inject into a vein or muscle. Always use a new needle for each injection. Check that the insulin looks clear and colorless before using — do not use it if it looks cloudy, colored, or has particles in it.
dosing: Your doctor will set your exact dose based on your blood sugar levels, meals, and individual needs. Insulin glulisine is usually injected 0 to 15 minutes BEFORE a meal or within 20 minutes AFTER starting a meal. Always follow your doctor's dosing instructions. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your healthcare team first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, check your blood sugar level first. Do NOT take a double dose to make up for the missed one. Contact your doctor or diabetes care team for guidance on what to do next. Having a plan in place before this happens is a good idea — ask your doctor ahead of time.
storage: Unopened (unused) vials or pens: Store in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F / 2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze. Do NOT use if it has been frozen. Once opened (in use): You may keep the vial or pen at room temperature (below 77°F / 25°C) for up to 28 days. Keep it away from direct heat and light. Discard any unused insulin after 28 days, even if there is still some left. Do NOT store your pen with a needle attached.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol or eating fewer carbohydrates than usual without adjusting your dose, as this can cause low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Avoid injecting into the same spot every time. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel your blood sugar is low or you are not feeling well. Avoid skipping meals after taking your dose, as this can cause dangerous low blood sugar.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, fast heartbeat, extreme hunger, blurred vision, or fainting); signs of high blood sugar (increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, or fatigue); severe allergic reaction (rash, itching, swelling of face or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness); skin lumps, redness, or changes at your injection site that do not go away; or if your blood sugar levels are consistently out of your target range.
when_it_works: Insulin glulisine starts working very quickly — usually within 10 to 20 minutes after injection. It reaches its peak (strongest) effect about 1 hour after injection and lasts for about 3 to 5 hours. Because it works so fast, it is important to eat your meal right around the time you take it.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Blood sugar control is very important during pregnancy. Your insulin dose may need to change. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to insulin and have a higher risk of low blood sugar. Blood sugar should be monitored carefully. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver disease, your insulin needs may be lower. Talk to your doctor about monitoring your blood sugar more closely. Children: Insulin glulisine is approved for children 4 years and older with type 1 diabetes. Dosing is based on the child's individual needs as determined by their doctor.
